title: Professional Negotiation Idioms & Incoterms 2020 Definitions
description: Master nuanced business idioms used during international automotive fleet sales, dealer conferences, and cross-border commercial bargaining.
learning_objectives: Deploy idiomatic business metaphors with confidence in meetings and negotiations
Avoid literal translations of Czech idioms into English commercial discussions
Understand idiomatic nuances used by international fleet buyers and military procurement officials

questions.prompt: We have submitted our best possible CIF pricing; now the _____ is in their court to finalize the contract.

explanations.correct: 'The ball is in their court' is a classic negotiation idiom meaning it is now their responsibility or turn to take action.
explanations.wrong_A: Literal replacement that ruins the idiomatic expression.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech says 'míč je na jejich straně hřiště'. In English, the exact idiom is 'the ball is in their court'.

questions.prompt: To _____ the deal for the municipal fire department, we included three years of free spare parts and oil filters.

explanations.correct: 'Sweeten the deal' means to add extra incentives or perks to make a commercial proposal more attractive to the buyer.
explanations.wrong_B: 'Soften the deal' means to make terms less harsh, not add attractive bonuses.
explanations.wrong_D: 'Grease' (e.g. grease palms) implies bribery, which is completely inappropriate.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'osladit / vylepšit nabídku' translates to 'sweeten the deal' or 'sweeten the pot'.

questions.prompt: Both legal teams spent four hours in the boardroom trying to _____ out the kinks in the intellectual property licensing agreement.

explanations.correct: 'Iron out the kinks' (or 'iron out wrinkles/details') means to resolve small remaining problems or complications.
explanations.wrong_B: The phrase is 'hammer out an agreement', but with 'kinks' the fixed collocation is 'iron out'.
explanations.wrong_C: Literal welding metaphor not found in this idiom.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'vychytat mouchy / vyhladit nesrovnalosti' is translated idiomatically as 'iron out the kinks'.

questions.prompt: Let's stop discussing minor administrative details and get down to _____ tacks: what is the bottom-line price per vehicle?

explanations.correct: 'Get down to brass tacks' is a well-known English idiom meaning to focus on the essential facts or core issues.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'přejít k jádru pudla / k věci' translates idiomatically to 'get down to brass tacks'.

questions.prompt: Neither side was willing to compromise on delivery penalty rates, and the negotiations reached a complete _____.

explanations.correct: 'Reach a stalemate' (or 'reach an impasse / deadlock') means reaching a situation where neither side can make progress.
explanations.wrong_A: 'Check' is a chess threat, not a stalemate.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'patová situace' translates to 'stalemate' (e.g. 'reach a stalemate' or 'end in stalemate').

questions.prompt: Before we sign the final distribution agreement, I want to touch _____ with our homologation engineer regarding local emissions.

explanations.correct: 'Touch base with [someone]' means to make brief contact or confer with someone to update status.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'spojit se s někým / krátce to zkonzultovat' is very commonly expressed in corporate English as 'touch base'.

questions.prompt: Our sales team was caught off _____ when the competitor announced a 10-year chassis warranty at the trade fair.

explanations.correct: 'Caught off guard' means surprised and unprepared for an unexpected development.
explanations.wrong_A: 'Off hand' means impromptu or without prior thought.
explanations.wrong_B: 'Off track' means diverted from the subject.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'být zaskočen / nachytán na švestkách' translates to 'be caught off guard'.

questions.prompt: If we want to close this defense deal before fiscal year-end, we need to _____ a compromise that satisfies both ministries.

explanations.correct: 'Hammer out a compromise / agreement' means to negotiate persistently until a mutually acceptable solution is forged.
explanations.wrong_B: 'Knock off' means reduce price or stop working.
explanations.wrong_D: 'Break down' means collapse or fail mechanically.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'vyjednat po těžkém boji kompromis' is expressed as 'hammer out a compromise'.

questions.prompt: The foreign dealer was clearly playing his cards close to his _____ during the pricing negotiations.

explanations.correct: 'Play cards close to one's chest' means to be very secretive and cautious about revealing one's plans or real intentions.
explanations.wrong_B: Playing on the table means open transparency (opposite meaning).
explanations.wrong_D: Having something up one's sleeve is a secret trick, but the idiom with cards close is 'chest'.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'neodkrývat karty / držet karty při těle' translates to 'play one's cards close to one's chest'.

questions.prompt: I will send a follow-up email tomorrow morning to close the _____ on all unanswered technical questions.

explanations.correct: 'Close the loop' means to finalize, resolve, and confirm the conclusion of an open communication or task.
explanations.wrong_A: 'Close the circle' is a geometric phrase.
explanations.wrong_C: 'Ring' is not part of this idiom.
explanations.wrong_D: 'Close the circuit' is an electrical action, not an organizational communication idiom.

questions.cz_learning_point: Czech 'dotáhnout věc do konce a potvrdit to' is idiomatically 'close the loop'.
